title: Moving to Greenwich: Everything You Need to Know
excerpt: A comprehensive guide for anyone considering moving to the Royal Borough of Greenwich, covering neighbourhoods, transport, schools, amenities, and lifestyle.
content:
Why Move to the Royal Borough of Greenwich?

The Royal Borough of Greenwich is one of London's most compelling places to live, offering a rare combination of world-class heritage, excellent transport connections, diverse neighbourhoods, and a quality of life that rivals anywhere in the capital. Home to the UNESCO World Heritage Site at Maritime Greenwich, the iconic O2 Arena, the Royal Observatory, and some of the finest parks in London, Greenwich delivers culture, history, and green space alongside the practical advantages of modern city living.

With average house prices around £440,000, Greenwich also offers relative affordability compared to many parts of inner London, particularly for the quality of housing and amenities available. The arrival of the Elizabeth line at Woolwich and Abbey Wood has transformed connectivity, while the Woolwich Arsenal regeneration is bringing billions of pounds of investment to the borough's eastern areas. Whether you are a young professional seeking riverside living, a family looking for good schools and green space, or a couple seeking village charm with city convenience, Greenwich has a neighbourhood to suit you.

Transport Connections

Greenwich's transport infrastructure is one of its greatest strengths and has improved dramatically in recent years. The Elizabeth line, London's newest railway, serves stations at Woolwich and Abbey Wood, providing fast, direct connections to Canary Wharf, Liverpool Street, Tottenham Court Road, Paddington, and Heathrow Airport. This single addition has transformed the connectivity of the borough's eastern areas and is a major reason for the property price growth seen in Woolwich and Abbey Wood.

The Docklands Light Railway serves Greenwich Town Centre via Cutty Sark and Greenwich stations, offering quick connections to Canary Wharf, Bank, and Lewisham. Mainline rail services from Greenwich, Blackheath, Charlton, Woolwich Arsenal, Plumstead, and Eltham provide direct trains to London Bridge, Charing Cross, Cannon Street, and Victoria, with most journeys taking fifteen to thirty minutes. The Jubilee line is accessible at North Greenwich, adjacent to the O2 Arena, providing connections across central London. Bus services are extensive, and the borough's riverside location means boat services operate from Greenwich Pier to central London. For drivers, the A2, A102, and Blackwall Tunnel provide road links to the north and south.

Schools and Education

Greenwich has a strong educational offering that makes it particularly attractive to families. The borough is home to numerous Ofsted-rated good and outstanding primary schools across all neighbourhoods, from Greenwich Town Centre to Abbey Wood. Secondary schools include highly regarded comprehensive schools and academies, while Eltham in particular is known for the quality of its educational provision.

For higher education, the University of Greenwich occupies the magnificent Old Royal Naval College buildings in Greenwich Town Centre, creating one of the most spectacular university campuses in the world. The Ravensbourne University London, based at Greenwich Peninsula near the O2, specialises in digital media and design. These institutions contribute to the borough's cultural vibrancy and provide educational opportunities for residents of all ages. Independent schools in and near the borough offer additional options for families seeking private education.

Green Spaces and Leisure

Greenwich is one of London's greenest boroughs, offering an exceptional range of parks, commons, and natural spaces that provide residents with breathing room and recreational opportunities. Greenwich Park, a Royal Park and part of the UNESCO World Heritage Site, is the crown jewel, with 183 acres of landscaped gardens, ancient trees, a deer park, and the Royal Observatory at its summit. The park's panoramic views across the Thames to Canary Wharf and the City of London are among the most photographed in the capital.

Blackheath Common provides a vast open expanse popular with joggers, dog walkers, and kite flyers, while Charlton Park offers sports facilities, a community garden, and summer events. In the south of the borough, Oxleas Wood is an ancient woodland dating back eight thousand years, offering nature trails through oak, birch, and hornbeam forest. Eltham Palace gardens, Avery Hill Park and its Winter Garden, Plumstead Common, Bostall Woods, and Lesnes Abbey Woods near Abbey Wood all contribute to a green infrastructure that gives Greenwich residents unrivalled access to nature within London.

Culture, Dining, and Entertainment

Greenwich's cultural offer is outstanding. The Maritime Greenwich UNESCO World Heritage Site encompasses the Old Royal Naval College, the National Maritime Museum, the Queen's House, and the Royal Observatory, providing free access to world-class museums and galleries. The Cutty Sark, the last surviving tea clipper, is a unique maritime attraction. Greenwich Market, operating since the early nineteenth century, offers artisan food, crafts, and antiques in a covered market hall that draws visitors from across London.

The O2 Arena at Greenwich Peninsula is one of the world's busiest entertainment venues, hosting major concerts, sporting events, and exhibitions throughout the year. The surrounding area includes restaurants, a cinema, and the Up at The O2 climbing experience. Blackheath Village offers a refined dining and drinking scene, with independent restaurants, wine bars, and cafes that give it a cosmopolitan character. Woolwich's dining options are increasingly diverse, reflecting the area's multicultural community and regeneration-driven investment.

Living in Greenwich: Neighbourhood by Neighbourhood

Choosing the right neighbourhood is the most important decision when moving to Greenwich, and the borough offers genuine diversity. Greenwich Town Centre suits those who want heritage, culture, and river views on their doorstep. Blackheath appeals to families and professionals seeking village elegance with outstanding period housing. Eltham is ideal for families wanting suburban space, good schools, and 1930s homes with gardens. Charlton offers an affordable riverside alternative with a strong community identity.

Woolwich is the choice for those excited by regeneration and new development, with the Elizabeth line providing unbeatable connectivity. Plumstead offers the most affordable entry point to the borough with a community feel and improving transport links. Abbey Wood has emerged as one of the most dynamic areas, with the Elizabeth line transforming its prospects and new-build developments attracting a wave of new residents. Each neighbourhood has its own personality, and spending time in different areas before committing is strongly recommended.
